claims.text: Post-sintering annealing will improve the tensile ductility of HfZrTiTa0.53.
Post-sintering annealing will improve the uniform elongation of HfZrTiTa0.53.
Annealing will produce a relaxed, equiaxed submicrocrystalline grain structure with enhanced grain-boundary cohesion.
The annealed alloy will largely retain its high compressive strength and impact-triggered energy release.
The initial HfZrTiTa0.53 material was produced by rapid solidification followed by hot isostatic pressing.
The initial material has a fine-grained microstructure.
The baseline alloy has a yield strength of approximately 786 MPa and compressive strength of approximately 1314 MPa.
A terminal strain of approximately 13.5% represents limited tensile ductility in the baseline alloy.
The proposed intervention is vacuum annealing at approximately 900°C for about 3 hours below the full recrystallization threshold.
Annealing will make the grains more equiaxed, slightly coarser, stress-relieved, and more cohesive at their boundaries.
Annealing will relieve residual stress and cause grain-boundary relaxation and limited recrystallization.
Residual-stress relief and grain-boundary modification will reduce stress concentrations and promote grain-boundary sliding or twinning.
Reduced stress concentrations and increased grain-boundary sliding or twinning will enhance tensile ductility without significantly reducing strength.
The treatment will not significantly compromise the alloy's capacity to release chemical energy upon impact.
Uniform elongation will increase from a stated 13.5% baseline to approximately 18–20%.
Yield strength after annealing will remain within approximately ±10% of 786 MPa.
The annealed and untreated alloys will have similar impact-energy-release profiles.
The hypothesis is limited to room-temperature, quasi-static tensile testing near 10^-3 s^-1, quasi-static compression, and ambient-temperature impact testing.
Matched annealed and untreated specimens from the same batch will be tested in tension, compression, and impact.
Failure to obtain at least a 20% relative improvement in uniform elongation while retaining yield strength within ±10% of 786 MPa and equivalent impact-energy release will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The reported 13.5% value is first described as terminal strain and later used as the baseline for uniform tensile elongation. Terminal strain and uniform elongation are distinct quantities and cannot be interchanged without evidence.

The 786 MPa baseline is presented in the context of compressive properties, but the experiment measures tensile yield strength and applies the 786 MPa retention threshold without clarifying the loading mode.

Retention of compressive strength is part of the hypothesis, but the falsification rule imposes no threshold for the measured compressive strength, so a large compressive-strength loss would not necessarily falsify the stated hypothesis.
